thread.title: Special Participation E: Cheatsheet Attention and Diffusion
thread.content:
As part of exploring how AI can enhance our conceptual understanding in EECS 182, I experimented with using modern AI learning modes (ChatGPT Study Mode, Claude Learning Mode, Gemini Guided Learning, and standard LLM prompting) to build individualized pre-lecture learning tools.I’m sharing the prompt, output artifacts, and annotated interaction trace so you can use them yourselves and also see both the strengths and the failure modes of LLM-assisted studying.NOTE:the model occasionally implied citations (“as from class notes”) without pulling actual page numbers Some formulas were slightly rephrased—not incorrect, but not exactly matching lecture notationThe kernel attention explanation is correct conceptually, but slightly hand-wavey on the random feature approximationThe Prompt I Used
“Generate a comprehensive, exam-ready cheatsheet for Berkeley EECS 182 (Fall 2025), focusing especially on:Attention mechanisms (self-attention, cross-attention, multi-head attention, transformer architecture),Generative AI models with emphasis on Diffusion Models (forward process, reverse process, score matching, ELBO, denoising networks, sampling algorithms).The cheatsheet should prioritize mathematical clarity, include equations and derivations, use text diagrams, and be optimized for last-minute review.”
Note I also provided the homework and discussion associated with the previously mentioned topicsConclusion:Useful as a study tool, but not a replacement for primary sources (lecture slides, notes, HW derivations). You must still verify key formulas.
thread.document:
As part of exploring how AI can enhance our conceptual understanding in EECS 182, I experimented with using modern AI learning modes (ChatGPT Study Mode, Claude Learning Mode, Gemini Guided Learning, and standard LLM prompting) to build individualized pre-lecture learning tools.

I’m sharing the prompt, output artifacts, and annotated interaction trace so you can use them yourselves and also see both the strengths and the failure modes of LLM-assisted studying.


NOTE:
the model occasionally implied citations (“as from class notes”) without pulling actual page numbers
 Some formulas were slightly rephrased—not incorrect, but not exactly matching lecture notation
The kernel attention explanation is correct conceptually, but slightly hand-wavey on the random feature approximation

The Prompt I Used

“Generate a comprehensive, exam-ready cheatsheet for Berkeley EECS 182 (Fall 2025), focusing especially on:
Attention mechanisms (self-attention, cross-attention, multi-head attention, transformer architecture),
Generative AI models with emphasis on Diffusion Models (forward process, reverse process, score matching, ELBO, denoising networks, sampling algorithms).
The cheatsheet should prioritize mathematical clarity, include equations and derivations, use text diagrams, and be optimized for last-minute review.”


Note I also provided the homework and discussion associated with the previously mentioned topics

Conclusion:
Useful as a study tool, but not a replacement for primary sources (lecture slides, notes, HW derivations). You must still verify key formulas.
